entities.name: Umayyad Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Umayyad Mosque (Great Mosque of Damascus) is one of the oldest and most magnificent mosques in the world, built by Umayyad Caliph al-Walid I between 706 and 715 CE in Damascus, Syria. Constructed on the site of a Byzantine cathedral (itself built over a Roman temple to Jupiter), the mosque was the third holiest site in early Islam, the first great monumental mosque of the Islamic world, and the architectural prototype for mosques across North Africa and Spain.

Al-Walid I demolished the Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist — which Christians had shared with Muslims since the Arab conquest of Damascus in 636 CE — and built the Great Mosque incorporating the earlier structure's Byzantine mosaics and columns. The mosque contains the Shrine of John the Baptist, where Muslims believe the head of the prophet Yahya (John the Baptist) is buried, making it sacred to both Islam and Christianity.

The mosque's three minarets (the oldest surviving Islamic minarets) and its magnificent Byzantine-style mosaic program depicting paradise cities were revolutionary. The treasury dome supported on Roman columns and the Dome of the Eagle over the prayer hall created architectural innovations copied across the Islamic world. The mosque was a model for the Great Mosque of Córdoba, Al-Qarawiyyin in Morocco, and dozens of other mosques. In 2001, Pope John Paul II visited the Umayyad Mosque — the first pope to enter a mosque — praying at the Shrine of John the Baptist.
